title: Aqeedah Essentials
description:
A comprehensive study of Islamic creed (Aqeedah), covering the fundamental beliefs that every Muslim must know. From Tawhid to the Last Day, this course presents the authentic beliefs of Ahlus Sunnah wal Jama'ah as established by the Quran, Sunnah, and the understanding of the Salaf.

The Aqeedah is the foundation upon which all acts of worship are built. Without correct creed, even the most apparent acts of worship may not be accepted. This course draws from classical works such as Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah, Al-Aqeedah al-Wasitiyyah, and the Quran itself.

This course is designed for beginners and provides clarity on common misconceptions about Islamic beliefs. Each lesson includes authentic references and scholarly explanations to ensure a thorough understanding of the creed of Islam.
short_description: Learn the authentic Islamic creed (Aqeedah) with classical references and scholarly explanations.

modules.title: The Concept of Tawhid
modules.description: Understanding the oneness of Allah, the most fundamental concept in Islam.

lessons.title: What is Tawhid?
lessons.content:
Tawhid (monotheism) is the cornerstone of Islam and the most important concept in the entire religion. It means the absolute oneness of Allah (SWT) in His essence, attributes, and actions. The Shahada itself is a declaration of Tawhid.

Allah (SWT) says in Surah Al-Ikhlas: 'Say, He is Allah, [who is] One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is begotten. Nor is there to Him any equivalent.' (Quran 112:1-4)

Imam al-Tahawi (رحمه الله) wrote in Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah: 'Allah is One, not like anything He has created, nor is anything He has created like Him. Nothing is comparable to Him.' (Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah, Line 43)

Tawhid is not merely a philosophical concept but a practical reality that governs every aspect of a Muslim's life. It demands that all forms of worship - prayer, supplication, sacrifice, hope, and fear - be directed exclusively to Allah (SWT). Any act of worship directed to other than Allah is considered shirk (associating partners with Allah), which is the gravest sin in Islam.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The right of Allah upon His servants is that they worship Him alone and associate nothing with Him.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2856, Sahih Muslim 30). This hadith establishes that Tawhid is the primary right of Allah over His creation.

lessons.title: Categories of Tawhid
lessons.content:
The scholars of Islam have categorized Tawhid into three main categories, each addressing a different aspect of the oneness of Allah. Understanding these categories is essential for a complete grasp of Islamic monotheism.

1. Tawhid al-Rububiyyah (Lordship): This is the belief that Allah alone is the Creator, Provider, Controller, and Manager of all affairs. Allah (SWT) says: 'Indeed, Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs.' (Quran 39:62). This category was never disputed by the disbelievers of Makkah, who acknowledged Allah as the Creator.

2. Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah (Worship): This is the belief that all acts of worship must be directed exclusively to Allah (SWT). This was the main point of contention between the Prophet (peace be upon him) and the polytheists. They acknowledged Allah's lordship but worshipped other gods alongside Him. Allah (SWT) says: 'And they worship other than Allah that which neither possesses for them provision from the heavens and the earth nor do they have [any] authority.' (Quran 16:73)

3. Tawhid al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat (Names and Attributes): This is the belief that Allah has beautiful names (al-Asma' al-Husna) and perfect attributes (Sifat) that befit His Majesty. We affirm what Allah has affirmed for Himself and what His Messenger (peace be upon him) affirmed, without distorting, denying, or asking 'how' (bila kayf).

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah (رحمه الله) explained that these three categories are interconnected and inseparable. A person cannot truly achieve Tawhid in one category without having it in all three. The understanding of these categories forms the basis of correct Islamic belief and practice.

lessons.title: Shirk and its Types
lessons.content:
Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is the opposite of Tawhid and the gravest sin in Islam. It is the one sin that Allah will not forgive if a person dies without repenting from it.

Allah (SWT) says: 'Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills.' (Quran 4:48)

The scholars have categorized Shirk into three main types:

1. Shirk al-Akbar (Major Shirk): This is associating partners with Allah in worship. Examples include making du'a to the dead, sacrificing to other than Allah, and seeking protection from other than Allah. This type expels a person from Islam.

2. Shirk al-Asghar (Minor Shirk): This is associating partners with Allah in a lesser way. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'I am not afraid that you will associate partners with Allah, but I am afraid that you will compete with each other in worldly matters.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2511). Examples include showing off in worship (riya').

3. Shirk al-Khafi (Hidden Shirk): This is shirk that is not apparent, such as excessive love for worldly things that takes one away from Allah. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The love of the world is the root of every sin.' (At-Tirmidhi 2336)

The cure for shirk is sincere Tawhid, seeking knowledge, and making du'a to Allah alone. The Prophet (peace be upon him) used to say in his supplications: 'O Allah, I seek refuge in You from associating anything with You while I know, and I seek Your forgiveness for what I do not know.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 832)

modules.title: The Six Articles of Faith
modules.description: The six fundamental beliefs that every Muslim must hold: belief in Allah, Angels, Books, Messengers, the Last Day, and Divine Decree.

lessons.title: Belief in Allah and His Names and Attributes
lessons.content:
Belief in Allah is the first and most important article of faith. It encompasses belief in His existence, His oneness, His Lordship, and His exclusive right to worship.

Allah (SWT) says: 'He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.' (Quran 59:22)

The 99 Names of Allah (al-Asma' al-Husna) are derived from the Quran and Sunnah. Each name represents an attribute of Allah that His servants should know, love, and hope in. For example:
- Ar-Rahman (The Entirely Merciful)
- Ar-Rahim (The Especially Merciful)
- Al-Malik (The King)
- Al-Quddus (The Holy)
- As-Salam (The Source of Peace)
- Al-Mu'min (The Granter of Security)

Imam al-Tahawi (رحمه الله) wrote: 'Allah has described Himself in His Book and by the tongue of His Messenger. He did so in a manner that combines gentleness and majesty, without exaggeration or deficiency. Every attribute He has described in His Book is true and real, and we affirm it without distortion or resemblance.' (Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah, Lines 69-74)

The correct methodology in understanding Allah's names and attributes is to affirm what He has affirmed for Himself and what His Messenger (peace be upon him) affirmed, without denying any attribute, distorting its meaning, or asking 'how' it is. This approach was taken by the Salaf (righteous predecessors) and is the position of Ahlus Sunnah wal Jama'ah.

lessons.title: Belief in the Angels
lessons.content:
Belief in the angels (Mala'ikah) is the second article of Islamic faith. Angels are honorable servants of Allah (SWT) created from light. They worship Him continuously and carry out His commands.

Allah (SWT) says: 'Praise be to Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers with wings - two, three, or four. He increases in creation whatever He wills.' (Quran 35:1)

Among the most important angels mentioned in the Quran and Sunnah are:
1. Jibril (Gabriel) - the angel of revelation, who brought the Quran to the Prophet (peace be upon him).
2. Mikail (Michael) - the angel responsible for provision, rain, and vegetation.
3. Israfil - the angel who will blow the trumpet on the Day of Judgment.
4. Azrael (Malak al-Mawt) - the angel of death, who takes the souls of the deceased.
5. Munkar and Nakir - the angels who question the dead in their graves.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The angels were created from light, the jinn from smokeless fire, and Adam from what has been described to you.' (Sahih Muslim 2996)

Angels have various duties, including recording deeds (Kiraman Katibin), protecting believers, and carrying out divine commands. They do not have free will in the sense of disobeying Allah; they worship Him by His command. Belief in angels strengthens a Muslim's faith in the unseen and awareness of Allah's constant supervision over creation.

lessons.title: Belief in the Revealed Books and Messengers
lessons.content:
Belief in the divine Books (Kutub) and Messengers (Rusul) is essential to Islamic faith. Allah (SWT) sent prophets and messengers to guide humanity, revealing scriptures to guide them in matters of worship and daily life.

Allah (SWT) says: 'Indeed, We have sent revelation to you, [O Muhammad], as We sent revelation to Noah and the prophets after him. And We sent Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Descendants [i.e., Jacob's descendants], Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon. And to David We gave the book [of Psalms]. (Quran 4:163)

The major divine Books mentioned in the Quran include:
1. Suhuf Ibrahim (Scrolls of Abraham)
2. Tawrat (Torah) - revealed to Musa (Moses)
3. Zabur (Psalms) - revealed to Dawud (David)
4. Injil (Gospel) - revealed to Isa (Jesus)
5. Quran - revealed to Muhammad (peace be upon him)

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The first prophet was Adam, and the last was Muhammad.' (Musnad Ahmad, graded Sahih). There were approximately 124,000 prophets sent to various nations throughout history.

We believe that the previous Books were revealed by Allah but have been altered or corrupted over time. The Quran, however, is preserved in its original form as Allah promised: 'Indeed, it is We who sent down the reminder (Quran) and indeed, We will be its guardian.' (Quran 15:9)

The prophets were all human beings, not divine. They were chosen by Allah to deliver His message, and they were the best of humanity in their times. We love all the prophets equally and do not distinguish between any of them, as Allah commanded: 'Say, We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Descendants, and what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting [in Islam].' (Quran 2:136)

lessons.title: Belief in the Last Day and Divine Decree
lessons.content:
Belief in the Last Day (Yawm al-Qiyamah) and Divine Decree (al-Qadr) are the fifth and sixth articles of Islamic faith.

Belief in the Last Day encompasses belief in the resurrection, the accounting of deeds, the Scale (Mizan), the Bridge (Sirat), Paradise (Jannah), and Hellfire (Jahannam). Allah (SWT) says: 'The Hour is coming - no doubt about it - and Allah will resurrect those in the graves.' (Quran 22:7)

The Prophet (peace be upon him) described the events of the Last Day in detail, including the blowing of the trumpet, the resurrection of all creation, the gathering on the plain, and the distribution of the records of deeds.

Belief in al-Qadr (Divine Decree) means believing that Allah has knowledge of all things, has written them in al-Lawh al-Mahfuz (the Preserved Tablet), has willed everything that happens, and has created everything. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Everything has been decreed except piety (taqwa).' (At-Tirmidhi 2517)

Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah states: 'The Divine Decree (Qadr) is a secret of Allah that has not been fully conveyed to any creation. The closest of people to Allah in this matter are those who submit to it and do not inquire about its details.' (Lines 99-100)

Belief in al-Qadr does not negate human free will and responsibility. Humans have the ability to choose their actions, but Allah knows what they will choose and has created it. This understanding combines tawakkul (reliance on Allah) with taking appropriate means. The believer strives and works, trusting in Allah's wisdom and plan.

modules.title: Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah
modules.description: A study of the most famous Islamic creed, authored by Imam al-Tahawi, which summarizes the beliefs of Ahlus Sunnah wal Jama'ah.

lessons.title: Introduction to Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah
lessons.content:
Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah is the most widely studied and accepted Islamic creed in the Sunni world. It was authored by Imam Abu Ja'far al-Tahawi (321 AH / 933 CE) and summarizes the beliefs of Ahlus Sunnah wal Jama'ah.

Imam al-Tahawi began his creed with these words: 'This is the description of the creed (Aqeedah) of Ahlus Sunnah wal Jama'ah, upon which were the Companions of the Prophet, the Tabi'in, and those who followed them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.'

This creed was written to address the theological controversies that arose in the early centuries of Islam, particularly the debates between the Mu'tazilites (who denied Allah's attributes), the Khawarij (who declared Muslims as disbelievers for major sins), and the Ash'arites (who introduced new theological concepts).

The creed covers the core beliefs of Islam in a concise and clear manner, avoiding unnecessary speculation and focusing on what Allah and His Messenger have taught. It is a safe haven from the storms of theological innovation and a guide to the straight path of the Salaf.

Imam al-Tahawi's approach was to affirm the apparent meanings of the Quran and Sunnah without engaging in ta'wil (allegorical interpretation) or tashbih (resemblance of Allah to His creation). This methodology has been praised by scholars throughout the centuries and remains the standard for Islamic creed.

lessons.title: Key Passages from Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah
lessons.content:
This lesson examines key passages from Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah that form the foundation of Islamic belief.

1. On Tawhid: 'Allah is One, not like anything He has created, nor is anything He has created like Him. Nothing is comparable to Him. He is the One who has no equal, no rival, no likeness, and no counterpart. He is the True God, whose Lordship is acknowledged, and no other is associated with His Lordship.'

2. On Allah's Names and Attributes: 'He has always existed with His attributes since before creation. He did not gain anything in creating creation, nor did creation gain anything from His creation. He was not created because He existed before, and He did not cease to exist because of His creation.'

3. On the Quran: 'The Quran is the Speech of Allah, revealed from Him without resembles His creation. Those who claim that it is created are committing kufr (disbelief), because they have denied the attribute of Allah's Speech, which is His eternal attribute.'

4. On Intercession (Shafa'ah): 'Intercession is true and has been established by the Quran and Sunnah. The Prophet (peace be upon him) has been given the right of intercession, and we hope that he will intercede for his Ummah on the Day of Judgment, as stated in authentic ahadith.'

5. On Faith (Iman): 'Iman (faith) is affirmation with the heart, statement with the tongue, and action with the limbs. It increases with obedience and decreases with disobedience. However, it does not increase to the point of becoming perfection, nor does it decrease to the point of being nullified.'

These passages demonstrate the balanced approach of Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah - affirming what the Quran and Sunnah affirm while avoiding extremism in either direction.

modules.title: Common Misconceptions in Aqeedah
modules.description: Addressing prevalent misunderstandings about Islamic beliefs with authentic evidence from the Quran and Sunnah.

lessons.title: Misconceptions about Allah's Names and Attributes
lessons.content:
One of the most common areas of misunderstanding in Islamic creed is the proper understanding of Allah's names and attributes. Several misconceptions have arisen over the centuries.

Misconception 1: 'Allah does not have attributes; the names are merely metaphors.' This is the position of the Mu'tazilites and some modernists. The correct position, as stated in Al-Aqeedah al-Tahawiyyah, is that Allah's names and attributes are real and must be affirmed as they appear in the Quran and Sunnah.

Misconception 2: 'Allah is everywhere (hulul).' This is the belief of the Sufis who claim that Allah is literally present in everything. The correct belief is that Allah is above His Throne (al-'Arsh), as stated in the Quran: 'The Most Merciful [who is] above the Throne established.' (Quran 20:5)

Misconception 3: 'We must interpret (ta'wil) Allah's attributes because they resemble human attributes.' The correct methodology is to affirm the attributes as mentioned without asking 'how' (bila kayf) or making resemblance (tashbih). Imam al-Tahawi stated: 'We do not enter into any of this with analogy, interpretation, or speculation.'

Misconception 4: 'The Throne (al-'Arsh) is a metaphor for dominion.' The Throne is a real creation of Allah, as stated in the Quran: 'His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth.' (Quran 2:229). The scholars agree that the Throne is real but its true nature is known only to Allah.

Misconception 5: 'Allah laughs' means He is pleased, not that He literally laughs.' The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah laughs at two people, one of whom kills the other and both enter Paradise.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3465). We affirm that Allah laughs, as stated in the hadith, without making it resemble human laughter.

The key principle in understanding Allah's attributes is: 'Affirmation without resemblance, denial without distortion.' This approach was taken by the Salaf and remains the safest methodology in matters of creed.

lessons.title: Misconceptions about the Prophets and the Last Day
lessons.content:
This lesson addresses common misconceptions about belief in the prophets and events of the Last Day.

Misconception 1: 'Prophets are sinless (ma'sum) and cannot make mistakes.' The correct belief is that the prophets are protected from major sins and disbelief, but they may commit minor errors. Allah (SWT) says about Adam: 'Then Adam received from his Lord [some] words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, it is He who is the Accepting of Repentance, the Merciful.' (Quran 2:37)

Misconception 2: 'Jesus (Isa) was crucified and died on the cross.' The Islamic belief, based on the Quran, is that Allah raised Jesus to heaven and he was not crucified: 'Rather, Allah raised him to Himself.' (Quran 4:158). The crucifixion was made to appear so to the people.

Misconception 3: 'The Dajjal (Antichrist) is a metaphor for evil.' The Dajjal is a real person who will appear in the end times, as described in numerous authentic ahadith. The Prophet (peace be upon him) warned about him extensively and instructed Muslims to seek refuge from him.

Misconception 4: 'There is no physical punishment in the grave.' The punishment of the grave (adhāb al-qabr) is established in the Quran and Sunnah. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The punishment of the grave is real, and if it were not that you would not bury the dead, I would have made you hear the punishment of the grave.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1372)

Misconception 5: 'Everyone will enter Paradise eventually.' The correct belief is that some people will enter Paradise without account (bila hisab) due to Allah's mercy, while others will enter after being accounted for their deeds. Some disbelievers will remain in Hellfire forever.

Misconception 6: 'We will see Allah in Paradise.' Yes, the believers will see Allah (SWT) in Paradise without any barrier. Allah (SWT) says: 'On that Day, faces will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.' (Quran 75:22-23). This is a real vision, not metaphorical.

These misconceptions highlight the importance of seeking knowledge from authentic sources and following the methodology of the Salaf in matters of creed.

lessons.title: The Correct Methodology in Aqeedah
lessons.content:
Having studied the fundamentals of Islamic creed, this final lesson summarizes the correct methodology that every Muslim should follow in matters of Aqeedah.

The methodology of Ahlus Sunnah wal Jama'ah in matters of creed can be summarized in several principles:

1. Follow the Quran and Sunnah: 'And hold fast to the Rope of Allah all together and do not become divided.' (Quran 3:103). The primary sources of Islamic creed are the Quran and the authentic Sunnah of the Prophet (peace be upon him).

2. Follow the understanding of the Salaf: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The best generation is my generation, then the one after them, then the one after them.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2652, Sahih Muslim 1067). The Companions and early Muslims had the best understanding of the religion.

3. Avoid theological speculation (kalām): Imam al-Tahawi stated: 'We do not enter into any of this with analogy, interpretation, or speculation.' The Aqeedah is based on revelation, not human reason.

4. Affirm without distortion or denial: 'Say, 'We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us.' (Quran 2:136). We affirm what Allah has affirmed for Himself and what His Messenger has affirmed, without adding, deleting, or distorting.

5. Avoid being extreme: 'And do not make yourselves handless [by being stingy], nor by being completely lavish.' (Quran 25:67). The correct Aqeedah is balanced, avoiding both negligence and excess.

6. Unite upon the truth: 'And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them.' (Quran 3:105). The Muslims should unite upon the correct Aqeedah and avoid division.

7. Learn and teach: 'O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow.' (Quran 59:18). Every Muslim has a responsibility to learn and teach correct beliefs.

The scholars of Ahlus Sunnah wal Jama'ah throughout the centuries have unanimously agreed on these principles. By adhering to them, a Muslim can navigate the challenges of modern ideologies and maintain a pure and authentic Islamic creed.
